---
title: "Quiz: ratio imaging and the noise of a ratio"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. $R = I_A/I_D$: acceptor over donor channel of a biosensor, both under donor excitation.

---

**Q1.** A biosensor is brighter in the nucleus than in the thin cytoplasm. Does that mean the signal (say, calcium) is higher there?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What else makes a pixel bright?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. Brightness also depends on how much sensor is in the pixel: thickness, concentration, illumination, focus. All of these multiply both channels, so the ratio cancels them; only the ratio reports the sensor's state.
:::

---

**Q2.** $A = 100$, $D = 400$ after background subtraction. What ratio do you get if you forget to subtract a background of 50 in both channels?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Add 50 to each.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$150/450 = 0.33$ instead of 0.25: the offset pulls the ratio towards 1, more in dim pixels.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why does a ratio image without a mask show a "carpet" of extreme colours outside the cells?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What are both channels outside the cell, after background subtraction?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Outside the cell both channels are noise around zero. The ratio of two numbers near zero is huge, negative or undefined (in the limit a Cauchy-like distribution). Mask with a threshold on the summed intensity, or use an intensity-modulated display.
:::

---

**Q4.** A sensor has $K_d = 200$ nM, $R_\text{min} = 0.5$, $R_\text{max} = 2.5$. A cell shows $R = 2.0$. What concentration? And for $R = 2.0 \pm 0.1$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$c = K_d (R - R_\text{min})/(R_\text{max} - R)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$c = 200\cdot1.5/0.5 = 600$ nM. $R = 1.9$: $200\cdot1.4/0.6 = 467$ nM; $R = 2.1$: $200\cdot1.6/0.4 = 800$ nM. A 5 % error in $R$ gives −22 %/+33 % in $c$, and it gets worse towards $R_\text{max}$.
:::

---

**Q5.** The acceptor channel has 100 photons per pixel, the donor channel 400. What is the CV of the ratio? Which channel would you make brighter?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\mathrm{CV}^2 \approx 1/N_A + 1/N_D$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\sqrt{0.01 + 0.0025} = 0.112$, 11 %. The acceptor channel: it contributes 0.01 of the 0.0125. Doubling the acceptor photons gives 8.7 %, doubling the donor photons only 10.6 %.
:::

---

**Q6.** Over a region you can average the pixel ratios, or divide the summed channels. Which is better, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which pixels does each give the most weight?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The ratio of sums: it weights pixels by their brightness and divides two large, precise numbers. The mean of ratios gives dim, noisy pixels the same weight as bright ones and inherits the upward bias of each dim ratio (about $1/N_D$).
:::

---

**Q7.** In a time-lapse the ratio of a resting cell drifts slowly downwards. Name a cause that is not biology, and a control.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Two dyes, two bleaching rates.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The acceptor bleaches faster than the donor, so $I_A/I_D$ falls. Control: an unstimulated cell (or the pre-stimulus baseline) imaged the same way; fit the drift and remove it.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Use the delta method to show that $\operatorname{E}[A/D] \approx (\mu_A/\mu_D)(1 + 1/\mu_D)$ for independent Poisson counts.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Expand $1/D$ around $\mu_D$ to second order.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$1/D = 1/(\mu_D + \delta) \approx (1/\mu_D)(1 - \delta/\mu_D + \delta^2/\mu_D^2)$. With $A$ independent, $\operatorname{E}[A/D] = \mu_A\operatorname{E}[1/D] \approx (\mu_A/\mu_D)(1 + \operatorname{Var}(D)/\mu_D^2) = (\mu_A/\mu_D)(1 + 1/\mu_D)$.
:::

---

**Q9.** Why does a flickering lamp make each channel noisy but hardly the ratio?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the flicker do to the covariance of the two channels?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The flicker multiplies both channels by the same factor, which cancels in $A/D$. In the variance formula it appears as a positive covariance, which is subtracted.
:::
